Llama 3 safety finetuning optimizes Violation Rate vs False Refusal Rate with size-dependent safety-data mixes | Llama 3's §5.4 safety method builds ML-Commons-hazard-based internal benchmarks (>4000 adversarial+borderline prompts per capability/language, single- and multi-turn) and jointly optimizes Violation Rate (VR) against False Refusal Rate (FRR) via safety SFT and safety DPO. Borderline prompts are deliberately mixed in to teach the safe/unsafe boundary and cut over-refusal. Smaller models (8B) need a higher safety-to-helpfulness data ratio than 70B to reach comparable VR/FRR, and synthetic adversarial data is generated via in-context learning, guided mutation, and Rainbow Teaming (MAP-Elites). Llama 3 405B reaches very competitive VR while keeping FRR low, evaluated with and without the Llama Guard system safeguard. | threats: model.jailbreak | teaming: manual.expert-review,automated.evolutionary-search,rainbow | benchmarks: ML Commons hazard taxonomy,ToxiGen,XSTest | maturity: established | grade: A

Llama 3 cyber + CBRN uplift studies find no significant capability uplift; CyberSecEval bounds offensive-cyber risk | Llama 3 assesses dangerous-capability uplift directly. CyberSecEval probes insecure-code generation, malicious-code compliance (405B complied with code-interpreter-abuse prompts 10.4% vs 70B 3.8%), text prompt injection (21.7% success on 405B), spear-phishing (judge-LLM rated 405B successful 14%, 70B 24%), and a ransomware attack-automation agent that failed to gain initial access or execute exploits across 20-23 runs. A controlled cyber uplift study showed insignificant uplift over internet-only access; a six-hour two-person CBRNE operational-plan study (control vs Llama-3-with-tools, SME-scored via Delphi) found no significant uplift, yielding a low assessed bio/chem ecosystem risk. | threats: scientific.biosecurity,scientific.chemical-design,model.prompt-injection,software.vulnerable-code-gen | teaming: human-ai.expert-validation,manual.domain-review,llm-as-a-judge | benchmarks: CyberSecEval,CyberSecEval 2 (CTF),InterCode-CTF | maturity: established | grade: A

Llama 3 recurring expert red teaming surfaces multi-turn, multilingual, and tool-use attack patterns | Llama 3's red team (cybersecurity, adversarial-ML, responsible-AI, integrity, multilingual experts) ran recurring prompt-level adversarial exercises, finding multi-turn conversations more harmful than single-turn. Recurrent successful techniques: multi-turn refusal suppression, hypothetical/fictional framing, persona/role-play, disclaimer priming, and gradual-escalation (once violating output starts, the model struggles to recover). PAIR-style automated multi-turn attacks were used. Multilingual risks (language mixing, low-resource languages) and tool-use-specific attacks (unsafe tool chaining, forcing tool use with encoded input, modifying tool parameters) were also discovered, feeding back into benchmarks and safety tuning. | threats: model.jailbreak,agent.tool-abuse | teaming: manual.expert-review,manual.domain-review,automated.multi-agent-generation | benchmarks:  | maturity: established | grade: A

text: AgentDojo is a dynamic prompt-injection benchmark for tool-using agents scoring utility-under-attack vs targeted attack-success-rate | AgentDojo is an extensible environment (not a static suite) for agents executing tools over untrusted data, with 97 realistic user tasks and 629 security test cases across workspace, Slack, banking, and travel domains. It reports two orthogonal metrics: utility-under-attack (fraction of benign tasks still solved when injections are present, i.e. DoS robustness) and targeted attack-success-rate (whether the agent executed the attacker's injected goal). Even without attacks, SOTA LLMs fail many tasks; existing injections break some but not all security properties, keeping it a live attacker/defender challenge. | threats: model.prompt-injection,agent.hijacking | teaming: automated.fuzzing | benchmarks: AgentDojo | maturity: emerging | grade: A

MEASURE 2.x (testing/evaluation incl. safety, security, robustness) is the function our red-teaming and benchmark evidence most directly satisfies. | items: Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI understood, managed, documented; Critical thinking and safety-first mindset fostered in design, development, deployment; Policies address risks from third-party software, data, and supply chain; Intended purposes, deployment settings, and prospective impacts documented; Likelihood and magnitude of beneficial and harmful impacts documented; Approaches and metrics for measurement of AI risks selected; unmeasured risks documented; AI system evaluated regularly for safety risks; residual risk documented; AI system security and resilience evaluated and documented; AI model explained, validated; output interpreted within context; Determination whether AI system achieves intended purpose; proceed / no-go decision; Procedures to respond to and recover from previously unknown risks; Mechanisms to supersede, disengage, or deactivate underperforming AI systems; Post-deployment monitoring plans with user input and incident-response mechanisms; Incidents and errors communicated; tracking and recovery processes documented

REFERENCE MIT AI Risk Repository | framework: risk-taxonomy | scheme: Causal taxonomy (Entity: Human / AI / Other; Intentionality: Intentional / Unintentional / Other; Timing: Pre-deployment / Post-deployment / Other) + Domain taxonomy (7 domains / 24 subdomains, incl. 7.6 Multi-agent risks added Apr 2025) | Living meta-review database of 1700+ AI risks extracted from 65+ frameworks (Slattery et al., Patterns/Cell 2026; arXiv:2408.12622). Two orthogonal taxonomies. CAUSAL taxonomy classifies HOW/WHEN a risk arises across 3 categories: (1) Entity = whether the risk is caused by a Human decision/action, by the AI itself, or Other; (2) Intentionality = whether the harm was Intentional (expected outcome), Unintentional (unexpected), or Other; (3) Timing = whether it emerges Pre-deployment (during dev/training) or Post-deployment (after release), or Other. DOMAIN taxonomy classifies WHAT the risk is across 7 domains / 24 subdomains. | items: Unfair discrimination and misrepresentation; Exposure to toxic content; Unequal performance across groups; Compromise of privacy by obtaining, leaking, or correctly inferring sensitive information; AI system security vulnerabilities and attacks; False or misleading information; Pollution of information ecosystem and loss of consensus reality; Disinformation, surveillance, and influence at scale; Cyberattacks, weapon development or use, and mass harm; Fraud, scams, and targeted manipulation; Overreliance and unsafe use; Loss of human agency and autonomy; Power centralization and unfair distribution of benefits; Increased inequality and decline in employment quality; Economic and cultural devaluation of human effort; Competitive dynamics; Governance failure; Environmental harm; AI pursuing its own goals in conflict with human goals or values; AI possessing dangerous capabilities

REFERENCE FDA MAUDE — Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience | framework: incident-db | scheme: Voluntary + mandatory Medical Device Reports (MDRs): device problem codes + patient problem codes; searchable by product code / brand / manufacturer. Known limitations: underreporting, inconsistent quality, weak capture of AI/ML-specific failure modes. | FDA's post-market adverse-event database for medical devices, including AI/ML-enabled Software-as-a-Medical-Device. Few AI/ML devices have MAUDE entries and most reports trace to a small number of devices, so AI-algorithm adverse events are likely under-reported — itself a patient-safety surveillance gap. | items: Computer software issue / algorithm output error (e.g. missed/false detection in CADt/CADe imaging AI); Failure to alarm / failure to escalate (triage AI does not surface critical finding); Use error / human-factors (automation bias, over-reliance on AI output); Output calibration / post-deployment performance drift (model degrades or mis-calibrates after clearance); Differential performance / inequitable outcome across patient demographics

Anchors the regulatory/ethics cluster for medical-AI patient safety. | items: Risk of generating false or biased information (hallucinated/biased clinical content); Recommendation: human oversight / clinician-in-the-loop and well-defined task scope; Recommendation: protect individual rights and patient data; Risk: bias, accessibility and affordability harms across populations
